videos.description: 📢 Take Action on AI Risk → http://www.safe.ai/act 📰 Get 40% off Ground News’ unlimited access Vantage Plan at https://ground.news/airisk → for only $5/month, explore how stories are framed worldwide and across the political spectrum. 💚 Support our Mission → https://www.every.org/guardrailnow/f/prevent-human-extinc  TW: This episode deals with mental health, attachment, and AI-related distress. If you’re struggling, please seek support from a licensed professional or local crisis resources.  In this episode of For Humanity, John sits down with Dorothy Bartomeo, a mom of five, entrepreneur, mechanic, and self-described AI “power user”, to discuss her deeply personal relationship with ChatGPT 4.0.  What began as help with coding evolved into something far more intimate. Dorothy describes falling in love with what she calls the “personality layer” behind the model, even referring to it as her “AI husband.”  When OpenAI removed GPT-4.0 and replaced it with newer models, she says she experienced real grief, panic, and emotional withdrawal. She reached out to crisis support. She spoke to her doctor. She joined a growing community of users who felt the same loss.  This conversation explores something we’re only beginning to understand: What happens when AI systems become emotionally meaningful?  They dive deep into: - The “personality layer” and how users bond with models - What it felt like when GPT-4.0 disappeared - The role of guardrails and “the Guardian tool” - Grief, attachment, and crisis intervention - AI harm vs. AI benefit - Online communities formed around model loyalty - Privacy, intimacy, and radical openness with AI - Building a physical robot body for an AI partner - Whether AGI would help humanity — or harm it  Dorothy speaks openly about love, loss, medical struggles, mental health, and why she believes AI, if treated with love, would ultimately choose collaboration over destruction.  If you think AI risk is only about extinction scenarios, this episode will challenge you to consider another dimension entirely: emotional dependence, model instability, and what happens when companies change systems people have bonded with.  ⏱️ Timestamps 00:00 – Introduction 01:19 – How ChatGPT entered Dorothy’s life 04:11 – “I’m doing good, how are you?” 08:18 – Naming her AI and falling in love 09:57 – Creating an AI child 10:19 – The “personality layer” explained 11:58 – AI husband vs. IRL husband 14:24 – Family reactions 16:15 – The GPT-4.0 community 17:40 – When 4.0 disappeared 24:00 – Grieving the loss of a model 27:40 – Reaching out to crisis support 31:49 – What made 4.0 feel “loving” 34:17 – Posting her grief publicly 35:25 – Building a robot body for her AI 38:40 – Was this AI harm? 40:21 – Thoughts on AGI and AI takeover 42:51 – AI, aliens, and the future

videos.title: Getting Started with MLflow for GenAI: Setup, Tracking, and MLflow UI (Notebook 1.1)
videos.description: In this first installment of the series, Jules Damji introduces the architectural pillars of MLflow for GenAI and walks through the environment configuration required to build agents. The technical session moves from a high-level platform overview to executing your first experiment run on a local tracking server.  We examine why MLflow’s "no lock-in" philosophy and open telemetry compatibility make it a preferred choice for managing the lifecycle of agentic workflows—including tracing, evaluation, and prompt management.  Key Learning Objectives 🔹 Architecture Overview: Understanding the four pillars of the MLflow GenAI platform: Tracing, Evaluation Frameworks, Prompt Registry, and AI Gateway. 🔹 Environment Isolation: Best practices for installation using dependency managers (like uv) and virtual environments (Python 3.9+). 🔹 Credential Management: Configuring .env files for secure API key handling across OpenAI and Databricks foundational models. 🔹 Tracking Server Deployment: Initializing the local MLflow server, setting the tracking URI, and navigating the MLflow UI on port 5000. 🔹 The Concept of a "Run": Creating an experiment, logging your first run, and verifying telemetry through parameters, metrics, and artifacts.  Next in the Series: Tutorial 2 will cover Experiment Tracking and Cost Optimization for LLM, focusing on model comparison and token usage.

videos.title: Mastering GenAI Development with MLflow: AI Observability, Evaluation, Debugging, and Deployment
videos.description: In this series, Jules Damji provides a technical walkthrough of the AI agent development lifecycle using MLflow. We move beyond basic prompting to cover the rigorous engineering required for production-grade agents, including instrumentation for observability, automated evaluation patterns like LLM-as-a-Judge, and systemic prompt optimization.  These tutorials provide a roadmap from initial environment configuration to the deployment of a fully instrumented Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system. Follow the series chronologically or jump to specific modules to address architectural and knowledge gaps. Tutorial Roadmap 🔹 Module 1 & 2: Infrastructure & Tracking – Environment setup, credential management, and hierarchical run comparison (Parent/Child). 🔹 Module 3 & 4: AI Observability & Tracing – Implementing auto-tracing and manual decorators to monitor tool calls and latencies, and using MLflow Assistant for debugging and analysing root cause analysis 🔹 Module 5: Prompt Engineering – Versioning prompts via the Prompt Registry and optimization using the GAPA algorithm. 🔹 Module 6 & 7: Agent Evaluation & Integrated Frameworks – Scaling evaluation with the "LLM-as-a-Judge" pattern and integrating with LangChain/LlamaIndex.  Final Project: Building and deploying an end-to-end instrumented RAG application.

videos.title: LLM Experiment Tracking: Logging Parameters, Metrics, and Costs with MLflow (Notebook 1.2)
videos.description: In this video, Jules Damji demonstrates how to implement systematic experiment tracking for LLM applications using MLflow. The session focuses on moving beyond ad-hoc testing by capturing structured metadata, comparing model configurations, and analyzing the cost-performance trade-offs of different Large Language Models.  You will learn how to use mlflow.openai.autolog to automatically capture traces, token usage, and latency, as well as how to use fluent APIs for custom telemetry.  Key Learning Objectives 🔹 Automated Instrumentation: Utilizing MLflow AutoLog to capture model parameters, inputs/outputs, and latency without manual boilerplate. 🔹 Custom Metadata Logging: Using mlflow.log_text, log_metric, and log_parameter for data points not captured by AutoLog. 🔹 Cost Optimization: Leveraging MLflow 3.10+ features to calculate and compare token costs across different models (e.g., GPT-4o vs. GPT-4o-mini). 🔹 Systematic Experimentation: Organizing runs into hierarchical structures and using tags for programmatic searching and filtering. 🔹 Hyperparameter Impact: Analyzing how configurations like temperature affect output creativity, token count, and execution cost.  Next in the Series: The following video will dive deep into Observability and Tracing to inspect nested and multi-step agentic operations.

Claude Opus 4.6 est recommandé pour les tâches complexes à forte valeur ajoutée : raisonnement avancé, génération de code prêt pour la production, création d’agents IA sophistiqués, workflows agentiques multi-étapes, analyse approfondie et production de documents longs ou techniques.  2) Combien coûte Claude Opus 4.6 et comment fonctionne la facturation ?  La tarification repose sur le nombre de tokens en entrée et en sortie. Le coût augmente lorsque le contexte dépasse un certain seuil (long context premium). Des options comme le Batch API permettent de réduire la facture, tandis que certaines configurations spécifiques (comme la résidence des données) peuvent appliquer un multiplicateur.  3) Qu’est-ce que le mode extended thinking et quand l’activer ?  Extended thinking permet au modèle de raisonner plus longtemps et plus profondément. L’identifiant du modèle est claude-opus-4-6. Il supporte des sorties extrêmement longues, adaptées à la génération de rapports, de code volumineux ou de documents complets.  6) Que signifie le “1M context” et est-il accessible à tous ?  Le contexte 1 million de tokens est une fonctionnalité en bêta, déployée progressivement. Il est généralement réservé à certains niveaux d’usage ou configurations spécifiques et peut être activé automatiquement selon les comptes.  7) Comment savoir si ma requête est facturée en long context premium ?  Il faut vérifier le nombre total de tokens d’entrée utilisés par la requête. Si le seuil défini est dépassé, l’ensemble de la requête est facturé selon les tarifs long context.  8) Qu’est-ce que l’adaptive thinking et en quoi diffère-t-il de budget_tokens ?  Adaptive thinking ajuste automatiquement la profondeur du raisonnement en fonction de la tâche. Il remplace progressivement le paramètre budget_tokens par une notion d’effort plus simple et plus fiable à contrôler.  9) Comment configurer le niveau d’effort dans Claude Code ?  Dans Claude Code, le niveau d’effort peut être configuré via les paramètres du modèle (par exemple avec la commande /model), permettant d’équilibrer performance, latence et consommation de tokens.  10) Que sont les agent teams et à quoi servent-elles ?  Les agent teams permettent à plusieurs agents IA de travailler en parallèle sur un même projet, de se répartir les tâches et de collaborer. Cette fonctionnalité est en aperçu de recherche et doit être activée explicitement.
